comma_castle.intro: Commas aren't about where you'd 'pause' — they do only a few legal jobs. Learn the jobs and delete the rest.
rules: A comma may separate a list, set off an intro element, join two sentences WITH a FANBOYS conjunction, or surround non-essential info. It also separates coordinate adjectives (a cold, damp morning) and the parts of dates and places (Paris, France, in May). If it isn’t doing one of those jobs, cut it.
List: apples, pears, and plums. Intro: After lunch, we left.
Extra info that renames a noun needs a comma on BOTH sides — or none at all. Never just one.
My brother, a pianist, won. (comma before AND after)
Two complete sentences can't be glued with a comma alone. Use a period, a semicolon, or a comma + FANBOYS.
Wrong: It rained, we left. Right: It rained, so we left.
A clause that picks out which one you mean is essential and takes no commas; extra information takes a pair. One subject with two verbs (tasted the sauce and added salt) needs no comma before “and”.
The students who finished early left. (only those) The students, who finished early, left. (all of them)
comma_castle.trap: Never put a single comma between a subject and its verb. The tall man, ran. is wrong.

apostrophe_alley.intro: Apostrophes show possession or a contraction — they NEVER make a word plural.
rules: it's = it is / it has. its = belonging to it (no apostrophe). Expand to 'it is' to test.

One owner: add ’s (the dog’s bone). Plural owner already ending in s: add just an apostrophe (the dogs’ bones). A plural without an s takes ’s (children’s). Two people sharing one thing: mark only the last name.
One boss: boss’s office. Many: bosses’ offices. The children’s books. Ana and Ben’s car (one car, shared).
To make an ordinary plural, add s with no apostrophe.
Make a family name plural first, then possessive: the Joneses’ house. Time words take possessives too: a day’s work, two hours’ delay. Separate ownership marks every name: Ana’s and Lia’s bikes.
apostrophe_alley.trap: whose = possessive; who's = who is. Same test as its/it's.

fragment_forest.intro: A real sentence needs a subject, a true verb, and a complete thought. Miss one and it's a fragment.
rules: An -ing word by itself is NOT a main verb. If nothing is actually happening in a standalone way, it’s a fragment. A command is complete even with no written subject: Go. has an understood “you”.
Fragment: The team, working hard. Fixed: The team worked hard.

because, although, since, while, if make a clause unable to stand alone — it must attach to a full sentence. So do who, which and whose when they open a clause: Which surprised everyone. is a fragment.
Although it rained needs a main clause to finish the thought.
Two sentences fused with nothing, or only a comma, is a run-on/splice. Separate or add comma + FANBOYS.
Run-on: I ran I was late. Fixed: I ran; I was late.
fragment_forest.trap: A long phrase can still be a fragment. Length ≠ completeness — hunt for the real verb.

dash_dungeon.intro: Dashes, colons, and semicolons look fancy but follow strict rules.
rules: Dashes: a pair, or one at the end

A pair of dashes sets off non-essential info mid-sentence — like a pair of commas: open with a dash, close with a dash. A single dash can also end a sentence, introducing a final reveal or explanation.
The plan — bold and risky — worked. She knew who had taken it — her brother.
A colon must follow a COMPLETE sentence, then introduces a list, example, or explanation.
She packed three things: a map, water, and boots.

A semicolon joins two complete, related sentences. If a period fits there, a semicolon is legal. It also comes before a linking adverb (; however,) and separates list items that already contain commas.
It rained; the game was cancelled. We visited Lima, Peru; Quito, Ecuador; and Bogotá, Colombia.

No mark goes between a verb and its object or the “that” clause it introduces, or after “such as”. Parentheses work like a pair of commas: they close around the extra words, with no comma added beside them.
The survey found that most residents agreed. The mill (built in 1790) still runs.
dash_dungeon.trap: The words BEFORE a colon must stand alone. She packed: a map… is illegal.

verb_valley.intro: Two things get tested: does the verb match its subject, and is the tense consistent.
rules: Ignore words between subject and verb
Cross out prepositional phrases; match the verb to the true subject.
The box of nails IS heavy. (box is, not nails)
Don't switch tenses without a reason; follow the passage's timeline.
Wrong: He runs and then jumped. Right: He ran and then jumped.
each, every, everyone, neither, and 'the team' are singular.
Everyone has a ticket. Neither answer is right.

With either/or and neither/nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Along with and as well as do not make a subject plural. When a sentence is inverted (On the shelf sit two jars), find the subject after the verb. Use had + participle for the earlier of two past events, would have (never “would of”) for what did not happen, and learn the irregular forms: lie, lay, lain; swim, swam, swum.
Either the manager or the assistants have the keys. By noon they had swum three laps.
verb_valley.trap: In 'There is/are,' the subject comes AFTER the verb: There ARE many reasons.

transition_tower.intro: The right transition depends on the relationship between the ideas around it — so read both.
rules: Read the sentence before AND after
Match the transition to how the two ideas relate, not to the single sentence it sits in.

Contrast: however, but, yet, nevertheless, although. Cause/effect: therefore, thus, so, consequently. Addition: also, moreover, in addition. Example: for example, for instance. Likeness: similarly, likewise. Restatement: in other words, that is. Condition: otherwise.
It is cheap; however, it breaks easily. (contrast)
If the sentence already signals the relationship, a second linking word adds nothing — delete it. Keep the one link the logic needs.
transition_tower.trap: Don't pick a word because it 'sounds smart' — match the logic (contrast vs. cause).

equation_station.intro: Linear algebra on the ACT is fast if you isolate the variable and know slope.
rules: Undo operations in reverse: add/subtract first, then multiply/divide.

Between (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂): (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁). In y=mx+b, m is slope (the rate: how much y changes per unit of x) and b is the y-intercept (the starting value). Put other forms into y = mx + b before reading the slope.
Solve one equation for a variable and plug in, or add/subtract equations to cancel one.
Two lines with the same slope and different intercepts are parallel, so the system has no solution. Same slope and same intercept means infinitely many.
equation_station.trap: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number flips the sign: 5 − 2x > 1 → −2x > −4 → x < 2.

fraction_falls.intro: Fractions, percents, and ratios are the same skill in different clothing.
rules: change ÷ original × 100. 'Of' means multiply; 'is' means equals.
'Half of a third' = ½ × ⅓ = ⅙.
Multiply every part by the same number. In a:b, part a is a/(a+b) of the whole.
After a change, the new amount is a multiple of the original: a 20% discount leaves 0.8 × original. Divide by that multiplier to go back. Adding the percent to the new amount does not undo it.
fraction_falls.trap: A 20% rise then a 20% fall does NOT return to start: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 (4% lower).

geometry_grotto.intro: Most ACT geometry reuses a small set of formulas and angle facts.
rules: Rectangle l×w. Triangle ½bh. Trapezoid ½(b₁+b₂)h. Circle πr². Circumference 2πr; an arc is (angle/360) of it. For a shaded region, subtract the inner area from the outer.
Box lwh. Cylinder πr²h. The ACT prints harder formulas such as the sphere’s (4/3)πr³ — your job is to substitute carefully. Break odd shapes into known pieces.
Straight line 180°, triangle 180°, circle 360°. Parallel lines cut by a transversal make angles that are equal or supplementary; the two interior angles on one side add to 180°.
The interior angles of an n-sided polygon add to (n − 2) × 180°. If two figures are similar with scale factor k, lengths scale by k, areas by k², and volumes by k³.
Hexagon: 4 × 180° = 720°. Double every side → 4 × the area.
geometry_grotto.trap: Diameter = 2r. Given diameter 10, use r=5 before πr².

function_foundry.intro: f(x) is just a machine: put a number in, follow the rule, read the number out.
rules: Replace every x with the input and compute.
For f(g(x)), evaluate g first, then feed that into f.
f(x)+k moves up k. f(x−h) moves RIGHT h — inside the parentheses is horizontal and opposite the sign.
The domain is every allowed input; the range is every possible output. An inverse undoes the function: swap x and y, then solve for y.

From a table, the change in f(x) per step in x is the slope. A piecewise function uses whichever rule matches the input. −f(x) reflects the graph across the x-axis; f(−x) reflects it across the y-axis. A relation is a function only if no input has two outputs.
function_foundry.trap: f(x−3) shifts RIGHT by 3, not left. Inside-the-parentheses changes go opposite the sign.

trig_trench.intro: Right-triangle trig is three ratios and a couple of special triangles.
rules: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj — all relative to the angle you're asked about.
180° = π radians. On the unit circle, cos is the x-coordinate, sin is the y-coordinate.

sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every angle. In the second quadrant (90° to 180°) sine is positive and cosine negative. To find a missing side, write the ratio as an equation and solve: cos θ = 10/h → h = 10 ÷ cos θ.
Angle of elevation 40°, 30 m away: height = 30 tan 40°.
trig_trench.trap: Opp and adj are defined relative to the specific angle in the question — re-check which angle.

probability_peaks.intro: Probability is a count: what you want over everything that could happen.
rules: Count the outcomes you want over all equally likely outcomes.
Independent events together → multiply. Either/or → add, then subtract anything counted twice. When the question fixes a group (“a 10th-grader is chosen”), that group is the new total.
P(at least one) = 1 − P(none). Usually far faster than listing cases.
At least one head in 2 flips: 1 − ¼ = ¾.
Multiply the number of choices at each step. When order does not matter, divide by the number of orderings. Expected value = each payout × its probability, added up.
probability_peaks.trap: Without replacement, the total shrinks each draw: 5/10 then 4/9, not 5/10 twice.

vocab_vault.intro: The ACT tests what a word means in THIS sentence — often a second, quieter meaning.
rules: Read the whole sentence; the word’s most familiar meaning is often the trap.
a novel solution → novel = new, not a book.
Cover the word, predict your own plain word, then match the closest option.
Positive context needs a positive word; negative needs negative. Cut mismatched tone.
Many tested words have a common meaning and a quieter one: currency can mean acceptance, telling can mean revealing, arrest can mean stop. Swap your choice into the sentence to check it.
The ice arrested the ship’s progress → halted.
vocab_vault.trap: Put your choice back into the sentence. If the sentence no longer means what the passage means, the choice is wrong, however well it matches the dictionary.

main_idea_meadow.intro: The main idea is the point of the WHOLE passage — not one detail, not the universe.
rules: The thesis usually sits in the opening or closing lines — read those closely.
Topic sentence + conclusion often state the point.
The right answer covers the entire passage: not a single example, not all of humanity.
One example = too narrow; 'life itself' = too broad.

Ask why it was written: to inform, argue, describe, or persuade. For a title, choose the one that fits every paragraph. A passage that opens “It is true that … But” puts its real point after the “But”.
An op-ed argues; a nature piece describes.
main_idea_meadow.trap: A true detail can still be the WRONG answer if it isn't the main point.

detail_desert.intro: Detail questions are open-book. The answer is right there — go get it.
rules: Reread the paragraph the question points to, and its neighbors; never answer from memory.
In the third paragraph… → reread the third paragraph.

The right answer usually restates the text in different words. A choice that copies the text’s words can be right, but check that it says what the text says — copied words are often used to dress up a wrong claim.
Wrong answers swap one word (all→some, always→often) or keep only half of a pair joined by “and”. On EXCEPT questions, tick each choice off against the text; the answer is the one you cannot find.
detail_desert.trap: Extreme words — always, never, all, none — are usually wrong unless the text says exactly that.

inference_icefield.intro: An inference is a tiny step past the text — strongly implied, never a wild guess.
rules: The right answer is barely beyond the words on the page.
She sighed and closed the book. → she's finished/tired, not 'she hates reading forever.'
If you cannot point to the sentence that forces it, it’s wrong. Harder inferences combine two statements: “only two things were checked” + “one passed” → the other failed.
Find the line that makes the conclusion unavoidable.
Cross out options that are too strong or reach beyond the passage.
inference_icefield.trap: 'Could be true' isn't enough — the answer must be BEST supported by the passage.

viewpoint_vista.intro: Paired passages test whether you can keep two voices straight and compare them.
rules: Before comparing, jot each author's main claim and tone in a word or two.
Questions ask where they would agree, what both assume, what both would reject, how one would answer the other, or which new evidence would favour one side.
Both value X, but split on Y.
Track which idea belongs to which passage; don't blend them.
Attribute every opinion to the right author.
viewpoint_vista.trap: An answer true for Passage A may be false for B — check BOTH before choosing 'both authors.'

data_delta.intro: Data questions are a scavenger hunt. Read the labels, then find the number.
rules: Note what each axis or column measures and its units before anything else.
State the direction. The ACT loves ‘increases, then decreases’ (a peak). A flat column is a finding too: that variable made no difference. Growing jumps mean a curve that steepens.
For an in-between value, estimate between the two nearest results. Past the last point, extend the trend (extrapolate) — the answer should keep going the way the data were going.
When no single table answers the question, find the shared column and carry the value across. A value far from its repeats is an outlier worth doubting.
data_delta.trap: Don't bring outside science — the answer is in the table/graph unless told otherwise.

graph_gorge.intro: Graphs add curves and crossings, but the reading skill is the same.
rules: Track one curve at a time
Use the legend and follow the single labeled curve you need.
Find the 'Trial 2' line, then read its y at the given x.
Where two curves cross, the two quantities are equal at that x-value.
Curves cross at x=5 → both equal there.

Check what each axis measures before reading a shape: a flat line on a velocity graph means constant speed, on a distance graph it means at rest. Watch uneven scales, and treat overlapping error bars as “no clear difference”.
If x goes 0, 10, 100, the scale isn't linear.
graph_gorge.trap: Read the value off the CORRECT axis — swapping x and y is the classic error.

experiment_expanse.intro: Every experiment question is really about variables and controls.
rules: Independent = what they change. Dependent = what they measure. Control/constant = what stays the same.
Changing temp, measuring yield → temp is independent.
The control is the no-treatment baseline that isolates the effect.
A no-drug group shows what happens without the drug.

If one variable changes, use the existing trend to predict the result. To extend a finding to a new condition, repeat the same test changing only that condition. Timing many repeats at once shrinks the error per repeat.
Higher temp raised yield → a hotter trial likely reads higher.
experiment_expanse.trap: Only ONE variable should change between trials. If two changed, you can't isolate a cause.

conflict_canyon.intro: Conflicting-viewpoints passages are a debate. Know each side's claim.
rules: One line per scientist: what they think and why.
Sci 1: the cause is A. Sci 2: the cause is B.
Note what both agree on — questions usually hinge on the disagreement.
Both agree it happened; they differ on the cause.

Match new evidence to the viewpoint it supports or weakens. Ask what each view predicts: an observation one view predicts and the other does not is the one that tells them apart. Evidence consistent with both decides nothing.
conflict_canyon.trap: Don't merge the theories — each answer must fit ONE scientist's specific view.

outside_outpost.intro: A handful of science facts are fair game. Memorize the few, then trust the data.
rules: pH < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic. Density = mass/volume. Photosynthesis: CO₂ + H₂O + light → sugar + O₂.
pH 3 is acidic; pH 10 is basic.

At sea level, water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C. Mitochondria release the energy stored in food; DNA stores genetic information. A Tt × tt cross gives half tt. Heating a gas in a rigid container raises its pressure.
Most questions live in the passage. Reach for outside knowledge only when the question needs it.
If the graph answers it, don't overthink.
outside_outpost.trap: Don't override clear passage data with a half-remembered fact — the data wins.

pronoun_pass.intro: A pronoun must clearly match its noun in number and use the right case.
rules: Singular nouns need singular pronouns. each, everyone and a company are singular.
The company raised its prices (not ‘their’). Each robot has its own station.
I/he/she/they are subjects; me/him/her/them are objects. Remove the other person to test.
between you and me — try 'between me,' not 'between I.'
Every pronoun must point to ONE obvious noun; vague it/they/this is wrong.
The car hit the pole, and it broke. — which broke? Fix it.
Do not switch from “one” to “you” or “they” partway through. Before a noun, test we/us by dropping the noun: thanked us students → thanked us. Nouns joined by “or” take a singular pronoun.
When one travels, one should carry a passport. Either Tom or Raj left his jacket.
pronoun_pass.trap: who = subject, whom = object. To whom — whom is the object of 'to.'

modifier_marsh.intro: A modifier must sit right next to the word it describes, or the sentence says something absurd.
rules: An opening phrase — an -ing or -ed phrase, a “to” phrase, or a noun phrase — must describe the subject right after the comma. A possessive (Maria’s seat) cannot be that subject.
Wrong: Running late, the bus was missed. Right: Running late, I missed the bus.
only, almost, just change meaning by position — put them next to what they limit.
I ate only one vs. I only ate one.
Long phrases drift; move them beside the noun they modify.
cookies for the kids on paper plates — who's on plates?
modifier_marsh.trap: After an intro phrase, the FIRST noun must be the thing doing the action.

parallel_pier.intro: Items joined in a list or by and/or must share the same grammatical form.
rules: Keep a list all -ing, all 'to ___', or all plain.
not only…but also, either…or, both…and, between…and, and not…but need parallel parts on each side.
Her score is higher than his score.
parallel_pier.trap: Check every item against the first — one mismatch breaks parallelism.

exponent_expanse.intro: Exponent rules turn scary powers into quick arithmetic.
rules: Rewrite both sides with the same base, then set exponents equal. In scientific notation multiply the front numbers and add the powers of 10. Simplify roots before adding them, and clear a root from a denominator by multiplying top and bottom by it.
exponent_expanse.trap: A negative exponent means reciprocal, NOT a negative number: 2⁻² = 1/4.

quadratic_quarry.intro: Most ACT quadratics factor cleanly or fall to the formula.
rules: Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. When the leading coefficient is not 1, check by expanding. Going the other way, a root r comes from the factor (x − r). Expanding (x + a)² gives x² + 2ax + a² — never forget the middle term.
If (x−a)(x−b) = 0, then x = a or x = b.
The discriminant b²−4ac counts the real roots.

y = a(x − h)² + k has its vertex at (h, k). If a > 0 the parabola opens up and the vertex is a minimum; if a < 0 it opens down and the vertex is a maximum. In standard form y = ax² + bx + c, the vertex is at x = −b/(2a).
quadratic_quarry.trap: Set the equation to 0 first. x² = 9 has TWO answers: x = 3 AND x = −3.

statistics_summit.intro: Know the three averages and how an outlier moves them.
rules: Sum the values, divide by how many.
Sort first, then take the middle (or average the two middles).
The value that shows up most.
To find a missing value or combine groups of different sizes, turn averages into totals first: total = mean × number of values.
Four tests average 82 → 328. To average 84 over five → 420, so the fifth is 92.

Standard deviation measures distance from the mean: adding the same number to every value leaves it unchanged. A percentile is a rank — the share of scores at or below yours — not a percentage correct. In a frequency table, count through the frequencies to find the middle value.
10, 10, 10, 10 and 1, 5, 15, 19 share a mean of 10; the second is far more spread out.
statistics_summit.trap: An outlier pulls the MEAN a lot but barely moves the MEDIAN.

coordinate_cove.intro: The coordinate plane has two must-know formulas.
rules: M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2). Given a midpoint and one end, step the same distance past the midpoint to find the other end.
Uphill left→right positive; downhill negative; flat 0; vertical undefined.
A line falling to the right has negative slope.
Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals. A circle with centre (h, k) and radius r is (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².

Reflecting across the y-axis changes the sign of x; across the x-axis, the sign of y. Two lines meet where their y-values are equal, so set the right-hand sides equal. A line with one y for every point is horizontal: y = constant.
coordinate_cove.trap: Distance needs the SQUARE root at the end — don't forget it.

structure_span.intro: Questions ask how a passage is organized or how a part functions.
rules: A history piece is often chronological.
Ask its job: introduce, support, counter, or conclude.
A middle paragraph often backs the thesis with an example.
however, yet, still = shift; for example = support; then = a turn in time; finally = conclusion. A question the author asks and then answers sets up an explanation.
structure_span.trap: A 'function' question asks WHY a line is there, not what it literally says.

tone_tundra.intro: Tone is the author's attitude, shown through word choice.
rules: Positive, negative, or neutral? Loaded words give it away — and irony is praise that the rest of the sentence undercuts (generously agreed to fix what it broke). Tone can shift inside a passage, so check the start and the end.
Most ACT tone is mild: appreciative, skeptical — not furious.
Overall attitude beats one dramatic line.
One harsh word doesn't make the tone 'angry.'
tone_tundra.trap: Extreme tone words (hateful, overjoyed) are usually wrong — the ACT stays moderate.

evidence_estuary.intro: Evidence questions ask how a detail bears on a claim: does it support it, weaken it, or complicate it?
rules: Before judging a piece of evidence, state the exact claim it bears on. Evidence supports a claim only if it makes that claim more likely.
Claim: the bridge brought customers. Most new customers crossed it on foot → supports.

Evidence weakens a claim when it points to another cause, shows the effect without the cause, or reverses the order of events; it strengthens it most when removing the cause removes the effect. It complicates a claim when it fits part of it but not all.
Sales also rose in towns with no bridge → weakens.
A result from a small or unusual group may not apply to everyone. Ask whether the sample matches the claim’s scope.
A survey of one school cannot settle a claim about all teenagers.
evidence_estuary.trap: Evidence that is merely about the same topic is not support. It has to change how likely the claim is.

figurative_falls.intro: The ACT sometimes asks what an image or comparison means.
rules: Read what the comparison represents, not the literal words. Also know personification (a house that holds its breath), hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration) and understatement (saying much less than the truth, often for humour).
Context tells you what the figure means here.
A 'storm' might mean conflict, not weather.
A warm image implies a positive idea; a dark one, negative.
figurative_falls.trap: Don't take figurative language literally — pick the meaning, not the picture.

units_uplands.intro: Half of science mistakes are really unit mistakes.
rules: Note the unit on each axis or column before comparing.
g vs. mg matters — 1 g = 1000 mg.
Watch prefixes: kilo = ×1000, milli = ÷1000. Area units convert by the square of the factor (1 m² = 10 000 cm²), and units combine the way the numbers do (force ÷ area → N/m²).
The same amount is a smaller number in a bigger unit.
micro (µ) = one millionth (÷ 1,000,000); nano (n) = one billionth. Count the zeros before converting.
units_uplands.trap: Never compare values in different units — convert to the same unit first.

rates_ridge.intro: Rates compare two quantities: miles per hour, grams per trial.
rules: Multiply the rate by the new amount.

Average rate = total amount ÷ total time. Do not average two rates unless they lasted equally long. Rates working together add (a leak subtracts); for two pumps, add the fractions of the job each does per hour.
60 km in 1 h, then 60 km in 2 h → 120 km ÷ 3 h = 40 km/h, not 45.
rates_ridge.trap: Match units before multiplying — don't mix hours with minutes.

hypothesis_hollow.intro: Science questions test whether results support a prediction.
rules: It predicts a result you can check with data, names what will change and what will be measured, and could turn out false. When two things rise together, consider a third factor driving both.
Compare the data to the prediction: match or not?
If growth rose with light, the data supports it.
A model is a useful approximation and can be updated.
New results can revise a model.
hypothesis_hollow.trap: Data that fits a prediction 'supports' it — it doesn't 'prove' it forever.

calc_canyon.intro: Some data questions want a quick calculation, not just a lookup.
rules: Locate the exact numbers in the table before computing.

Subtract for change; divide by the original for percent change. For a share, divide the part by the whole. For a rate between two rows, divide the change in one column by the change in the other. When mixing, weight each value by how much there is of it.
Add the values and divide by how many.
calc_canyon.trap: Use the exact rows asked about — don't average the whole table by accident.
